lessons.title: Case Study: How Export Sectors Reacted to Rupee Depreciation

body.text: A weaker rupee is a tailwind for exporters, not an investment thesis. In some episodes Indian IT and pharma stocks soared as the rupee fell. In another, IT stocks crashed while the rupee hit record lows. The difference was never the currency itself. It was what was happening to demand for the exporters' products at the same time.

children.text: The last two lessons explained, in theory, why a weaker rupee helps IT services and pharma exporters. This case study tests that theory against three real episodes of sharp rupee depreciation: the 2013 taper tantrum, the 2018 slide, and the 2022 fall to record lows. You will see where the textbook held, where it broke, and the checklist that separates the two.

body.title: Approximate Rise in USD/INR From Start to Low Point of Each Episode (%)

events.title: The taper signal
events.description: US Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke indicated the Fed could begin slowing its bond purchases. Foreign investors began pulling money out of emerging markets, especially those with large current account deficits.

events.title: Pressure builds on India
events.description: With a wide current account deficit and high inflation, India was grouped among the most vulnerable economies. The RBI tightened short-term liquidity in July to defend the rupee, pushing up short-term rates.

events.title: Record low
events.description: The rupee fell to a then-record low of close to 69 against the dollar, from around 55 in early May.

events.title: New RBI Governor
events.description: Raghuram Rajan took charge as RBI Governor and announced measures including a special swap window to attract foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians. Sentiment turned.

events.title: Partial recovery
events.description: The rupee recovered to the low 60s. Over the year, IT and pharma exporters were among the strongest performing sectors on NSE, while rate-sensitive and import-dependent sectors struggled.

children.text: In 2013, the textbook worked. US demand for IT outsourcing was stable and growing as the US economy recovered, and Indian pharma companies were winning a steady stream of US generic approvals. The currency tailwind landed on top of healthy demand, so both revenue and margins improved. Investors rotated into exporters as a hedge against the domestic slowdown and a falling rupee.

The flip side of an export windfall is an import shock. Oil marketing companies faced higher rupee costs for crude. Companies that had borrowed in dollars through external commercial borrowings or foreign currency convertible bonds without hedging saw their rupee debt burden jump, hurting infrastructure, power, and some capital goods companies already weakened by the investment slowdown. Consumer durables and auto companies with imported components faced margin pressure. At the same time, the RBI's emergency liquidity tightening lifted short-term rates, hitting banks and other rate-sensitive stocks.

In 2018, rising crude prices widened India's current account deficit, the US Fed kept raising rates, and foreign investors sold Indian assets. The rupee slid from around 63.5 in January to past 74 by October. Large IT services stocks again did well, as US clients were spending on digital transformation and the currency added to margins. Pharma was more mixed: the rupee helped, but US generics were in the middle of a multi-year period of heavy price erosion caused by consolidation among US buyers, so the currency gain was partly swallowed by falling prices. The lesson from 2018: the tailwind lifts everyone equally, but it cannot fix a sector-specific problem.

In 2022, the rupee fell to record lows, crossing 80 in July and approaching 83 in October. By the textbook, IT should have been a star. Instead, as you saw in Chapter 1, the Nifty IT index fell roughly 26% for the year, one of the worst sector performances in the market. Three forces overwhelmed the currency tailwind.

body.title: Why the Rupee Helped IT in 2013 but Not in 2022

columns.label: 2013: tailwind plus healthy demand
points: US economy recovering and technology spending steady
IT stocks had not been bid up to extreme valuations
Result: exporters were among the best performers

columns.label: 2022: tailwind against three headwinds
points: Aggressive US Fed hikes raised fears of a US recession and cuts to discretionary tech budgets
IT stocks entered the year at very high valuations after the 2021 boom, so slowing growth hit multiples hard
Record attrition and wage inflation absorbed much of the currency margin benefit, and a weak euro and pound reduced dollar revenue
Result: IT fell sharply despite a record-weak rupee

body.text: Markets price the future, and currency is only one input. When demand, valuation, and currency point the same way, exporters can soar. When the currency is the only good news, it rarely carries the stock on its own.

children.text: Two Things That Dilute the Currency Gain

markDefs.definition: A contract to exchange a fixed amount of foreign currency at a pre-agreed rate on a future date. Exporters use them to lock in the rupee value of future dollar revenue.

children.text: First, hedging. Large exporters sell a portion of their expected dollar revenue in advance through

and options, often for several quarters ahead. When the rupee falls suddenly, the hedged portion still converts at the older, stronger rate. The benefit arrives gradually as old hedges expire. Second, cross-currency movement. Revenue billed in euros, pounds, or Australian dollars converts into fewer US dollars when those currencies weaken against the dollar, as the euro and pound did sharply in 2022.

body.caption: The average USD/INR rate at which an exporter actually converts its dollar revenue, simplified

body.title: What Rate Did the Company Really Get?
body.prompt: An IT exporter has hedged 60% of this quarter's dollar revenue at USD/INR 76. The rupee has since fallen, and the spot rate during the quarter averages 82. The remaining 40% converts at spot. What effective USD/INR rate does the company realise on its dollar revenue? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Effective rate = (0.60 × 76) + (0.40 × 82) = 45.6 + 32.8 = 78.4. The spot rate moved 7.9% from 76 to 82, but the company's realised rate improved only about 3.2% over its hedge rate. Part of the remaining gain arrives in later quarters as older hedges roll off and new ones are booked at weaker rupee levels.

body.title: The Cross-Currency Hit
body.prompt: An IT company earns 30% of its revenue in euros and 70% in US dollars. In a quarter, the euro weakens 10% against the US dollar, and business volumes in constant currency are flat. Approximately how much does its US dollar revenue change? Enter the answer as a percentage, using a minus sign if it falls.
body.explanation: Only the euro portion is affected: 30% × -10% = -3%. So reported dollar revenue falls about 3% even though the company did exactly the same amount of work. This is why the 2022 dollar revenue growth of many Indian IT companies trailed their constant currency growth.

body.caption: How Exporters Fared in Each Episode, in Summary

cells: Healthy US demand plus currency tailwind
IT demand healthy; pharma held back by US price erosion
US recession fears, high starting valuations, wage inflation, and cross-currency losses outweighed the rupee

body.title: Apply the Lesson
body.question: The rupee falls 6% against the dollar over three months. Which additional condition makes it most likely that IT services stocks will outperform?
options: US clients are cutting discretionary technology budgets and IT stocks trade near record valuations
The euro and pound are falling faster than the rupee against the dollar
Deal wins are rising, attrition is stable, and IT stocks trade near their long-term average valuations
Most IT companies have hedged the next four quarters of revenue at older rates
body.explanation: The currency tailwind is most powerful when it lands on healthy demand, stable costs, and reasonable valuations, as in 2013. Option one describes 2022. Falling euro and pound rates cut dollar revenue. Heavy hedging at older rates delays the benefit.

body.title: The Rupee Hits a New Low
body.scenario: A business channel runs a breaking headline: 'Rupee hits all-time low against the dollar.' A guest analyst says, 'This is the time to load up on IT and pharma stocks.' You hold a large cap fund and are considering adding an IT sectoral fund.
body.prompt: What would you check before acting on the analyst's advice?
body.modelAnswer: Start by accepting that currency alone is not a reason to buy. Check demand: are US and European clients increasing or cutting technology budgets, and what do recent deal wins and management commentary say? Check valuations: are IT stocks trading near their historical average P/E or well above it after a strong run? Check costs: are wages and attrition stable, or rising and likely to absorb the currency gain? Check cross-currency: are the euro and pound also weakening against the dollar? Check hedging: companies' hedge books mean the benefit will arrive gradually. Check your existing exposure: your large cap fund already holds significant IT weight, so a sectoral fund adds concentration. If demand and valuations look supportive, the currency adds to the case. If not, the headline is noise.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Exporters that have ___ a large share of future dollar revenue at older exchange rates will see the benefit of a sudden rupee fall only gradually.
body.explanation: Hedged revenue converts at the pre-agreed rate, so a sudden rupee move only benefits the unhedged portion until old hedges expire.

body.title: Before Buying Exporters on Rupee Weakness
steps: Confirm demand is healthy: recent deal wins, client spending commentary, and constant currency growth trends
Compare current sector valuations with their five to ten year averages
Check wage inflation and attrition trends that could absorb margin gains
Look at the geography mix and whether the euro and pound are also moving against the dollar
Read each company's hedging disclosure to understand how quickly the benefit will show up
Check the other side of your portfolio: importers, oil-sensitive sectors, and companies with foreign currency debt
Ask whether the rupee move is already known and priced in before you act

points: A weaker rupee helps exporters, but it is a tailwind, not a thesis; demand and valuation decide the outcome
In 2013, healthy US demand plus a sharply weaker rupee made IT and pharma among the best performing sectors
In 2018, IT benefited again, while pharma's currency gain was partly offset by US generic price erosion
In 2022, IT fell sharply despite record rupee lows because of US recession fears, high starting valuations, wage inflation, and cross-currency losses
Hedging delays the currency benefit, and weaker euro and pound rates can cut dollar revenue
Every export windfall has an import side: oil marketing companies and companies with unhedged foreign debt suffer when the rupee falls
